extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students studying set theory/cardinality (exercises and hints)
extracted.subtask_description: Solve and justify textbook-style exercises about countability, bijections, equinumerosity, and related set-theoretic constructions; produce explicit formulas and rigorous proofs where requested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove a given function is a bijection
rubrics_metrics.description: You must prove that your function is a bijection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show injectivity and surjectivity (or explicitly provide the inverse). For functions like f : N → Z given by a case formula, prove the two properties for all inputs rather than giving only examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine (denumerable/countable/uncountable) status of a set
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine if each of the following sets is denumerable / countable / uncountable (e.g., irrationals, [0,1]∩Q, sets formed by adding/multiplying Q by a fixed real, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use known results (Q is countable, R uncountable), explicit enumerations, injections/surjections, algebraic manipulations, or diagonal-type arguments as appropriate. For sets built from Q and a fixed real a, consider translations and scalings; for sets like {π + q : q ∈ Q} use bijective translation by a.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct an explicit bijection to show equinumerosity
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that two sets are equinumerous by constructing an explicit bijection between them (examples include R and (0,1), R and (√2, ∞), (0,∞) and (0,∞) − {1}, R2 and R, (0,1)×(0,1) and (0,1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a formula for the bijection (not a mere table). Give full proofs of injectivity and surjectivity. When constructing bijections between intervals and R, common maps include fractional linear maps, tangent-type maps, or decimal-interleaving for products. Address non-uniqueness of decimal expansions (0.24999... = 0.25000...) when using decimal representations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide two distinct explicit bijections when requested
rubrics_metrics.description: Show R and (0,1) are equinumerous by giving two different explicit bijections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give two different formulas (for example: a bijection using tan/atan and another using a Möbius map or algebraic rational function). For each, prove bijectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Cantor diagonal argument to prove uncountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Let S be the set of all functions f : N → {0,1}. Prove that S is uncountable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Cantor's diagonalization: assume an enumeration, construct a function differing from the nth function at index n to produce a function not in the list. Emphasize that the codomain here has only two elements; the diagonal argument still applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe bijection with a formula (not as a table)
rubrics_metrics.description: Show two given sets have equal cardinality by describing a bijection from one to the other. Describe your bijection with a formula (not as a table).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give a closed-form or piecewise formula mapping elements and prove it is one-to-one and onto. Avoid ad-hoc finite listings; use algebraic or analytic expressions where possible (e.g., mapping even ↔ odd integers by n ↦ n±1 or 2n ↦ 2n+1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove unions of equinumerous/partitioned sets are equinumerous
rubrics_metrics.description: If A∩C = ∅ and B∩D = ∅ and |A| = |B|, |C| = |D|, show |A ∪ C| = |B ∪ D|. More generally, given partitions P of A and Q of B and a bijection h : P → Q with |X| = |h(X)| for each X, show |A| = |B|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct a bijection on each part (use given bijections or construct them) and combine them into a global bijection on unions, taking care about disjointness. For partitions, define the global map piecewise using the bijections on corresponding blocks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Cantor–Schröder–Bernstein (CSB) via injections
rubrics_metrics.description: When asked to show two sets have the same cardinality, consider defining injections both ways and applying Cantor–Schröder–Bernstein.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you can give injections f : A → B and g : B → A, CSB implies a bijection exists. The hint explicitly suggests for part (a) of some exercises: 'try to define an injection from each set to the other; you can then use Cantor-Schröder-Bernstein 12.5.1 to infer there is a bijection between the sets.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Show |P(A)| = |P(B)| when |A| = |B|
rubrics_metrics.description: Let A and B be equinumerous sets. Show that |𝒫(A)| = |𝒫(B)|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the bijection f : A → B to induce a bijection F : 𝒫(A) → 𝒫(B) via F(X) = {f(x) : x ∈ X}. Prove F is injective and surjective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Countability of sets of polynomials and their roots
rubrics_metrics.description: Show Pm (degree m polynomials with rational coefficients) is countable; P (all polynomials with rational coefficients) is countable; discuss cardinality of A = {real roots of polynomials in P}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue Pm ≈ Q^{m+1}  ackslash {leading_coefficient=0} is countable (product of countable sets). Use countable union over m to show P countable. For roots, use Fundamental Theorem of Algebra (each nonzero polynomial of degree n has at most n real roots) to relate |A| to |P|; consider whether mapping polynomials → roots is injective/surjective to decide |A| vs |P|.

rubrics_metrics.name: Countability of Fn = {X ⊂ N : |X| = n} and unions over n
rubrics_metrics.description: For each n ∈ N, |Fn| = |N|; also show ⋃_{n∈N} Fn has cardinality |N|, and explain compatibility with |N| < |P(N)|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For fixed n, give explicit enumeration (e.g., lexicographic) or bijection with N. For the union, express as countable union of countable sets and enumerate (diagonal or pairing). Explain that ⋃_n Fn is the set of finite subsets of N, which is countable, whereas P(N) includes infinite subsets and is uncountable; no contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Countable unions of countable/denumerable sets
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) Let A1, A2, ... be denumerable disjoint sets; show ⋃_{n=1}^∞ A_n is denumerable. (b) If A1, A2, ... are countable and disjoint show union is countable. (c) Remove disjointness assumption and still show countable union is countable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use explicit enumerations and the diagonal-sweeping argument (or bijection N×N → N) to list elements. When sets are not disjoint, adjust enumerations to avoid repeats or partition into disjoint representatives Bn as suggested in hints and then enumerate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use diagonal sweeping argument for N×N enumeration
rubrics_metrics.description: To enumerate countable unions or Cartesian products, use the diagonal sweeping argument (as in proof of Result 12.2.6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define an explicit pairing/enumeration (e.g., Cantor pairing or diagonal traversal) and prove it is a bijection. For unions, arrange elements in a grid and sweep diagonally, skipping repeats when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be careful with decimal representations when using digits to encode pairs
rubrics_metrics.description: When using decimal expansions to map (0,1)×(0,1) to (0,1), be careful: 0.250000... = 0.249999....
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid ambiguity by choosing a canonical expansion (e.g., disallow terminating expansions or disallow expansions ending in infinite 9's), or handle exceptional cases separately when defining the bijection. The hint explicitly warns about this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof techniques: contrapositive, contradiction, induction, modular arithmetic, Bézout, triangle inequality
rubrics_metrics.description: Use standard proof techniques depending on problem: contrapositive for supremum/minimality arguments, contradiction when negation yields easier deductions, mathematical induction for finite-structure claims, modular arithmetic and Bézout's identity for divisibility problems, triangle inequality for bounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The hints repeatedly recommend selecting the technique that simplifies the problem (e.g., to prove 'a is supremum' show it's an upper bound and that any b<a is not an upper bound; to show implication false analyze when hypothesis true & conclusion false). Use small examples to build intuition before generalizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about domain and codomain when testing injectivity/surjectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining if a function is injective or surjective, consider the domain and codomain carefully; a function is not just a formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check definitions: injective (distinct inputs give distinct outputs), surjective (range equals codomain). Use preimage notation f^{-1}(D) properly (it denotes preimage, not inverse function unless bijective). For compositions, remember: if f∘g is injective then g is injective; if f∘g is surjective then f is surjective.

rubrics_metrics.name: When proving set equality show two inclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: To show two sets are equal, show each is a subset of the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This classic technique is emphasized in function and set hints: prove A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A separately rather than trying to assert equality without justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mapping finite combinatorial constructions: use combinatorial identities and induction
rubrics_metrics.description: For counting finite combinatorial sets (binomial coefficients, factorial expressions) or proving combinatorial identities, use Pascal's identity, factorial manipulations, recurrence relations, and induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hints point to using factorial representations, double-factorial where useful, Pascal identity, and induction on n for sums/products involving binomial coefficients or factorials.
